blocks.text: It is proved that צמאון tsimmaon is not the dipsas, as some render it following Jerome, but a thirsty place, Deut. VIII, 15.

The dipsas is similar to the viper, but smaller, scarcely a span long, with a white body and a slender tail marked with two lines, which it raises upward as it moves, as the Arabs observe. All writers describe it in Africa. But some also place it in Arabia: Aelian, History book 6, ch. 51: Γίνονται δὲ ἄρα ἐν Λιβύῃ τε καὶ Ἀραβίᾳ μᾶλλον [Ginontai de ara en Libyē te kai Arabia mallon]. So also Suidas. And Gregory of Nazianzus, Iambic 22, places it in the deserts of Egypt:
Διψὰς τὶς ἐστι τῶν ἐχιδναίων γενῶν, Τούτων, ὅσ᾽ ἡ ἔρημος Αἰγύπτου φέρει· [Dipsas tis esti tōn echidnaiōn genōn, Toutōn, hos' hē erēmos Aigyptou pherei]

The dipsas is a serpent of the viper kind, one of those which the desert of Egypt produces. Others also place it in Syria. Avicenna, vol. 2, p. 139: وقال قوم ان اكثر ما تكون هذه في بلاد لوبية والشام [wa-qāla qawm anna akthar mā takūn hādhihi fī bilād Lūbiya wa-l-Shām] Some say that it is found mostly in the regions of Africa and Syria. In Aelian, some call it prester, [col. 398] others causon, and melanurus, and ammobates, and centris. But the common name is διψὰς [dipsas], from the insatiable thirst which its bite produces. Isidore renders it situla. And Avicenna uses a periphrasis, الحية المعطشة [al-ḥayya al-muʿṭisha], the serpent that causes thirst, as though it lacked a proper name. This is surprising, since it is said to be common in Arabia and in neighbouring places such as Egypt and Syria. Whoever wants more on this serpent should read, besides Nicander and the physicians, Aelian in the place cited above, Lucian in the book On the Dipsads, Lucan book 9, line 738, Nazianzen in the passage we have quoted, Epiphanius on the Marcosians, and Isidore, who, following Solinus, wrongly counts it among the asps, although it comes closest to the viper.

It is also found in Jerome's version of Deut. VIII, 15: "And he was your guide in the great and terrible wilderness, in which there was the serpent burning with its breath, and the scorpion, and the dipsas." But that the Hebrew word צמאון tsimmaon, rendered there dipsas, means something else, namely thirst, dryness, a thirsty place, there are many arguments that do not merely suggest but convince. First, the constant use of the word in the sense we have stated. Thus Psalm. CVII, 33: "He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water לצמאון, into a thirsty place." The Greeks: εἰς δίψαν [eis dipsan]; the Vulgate translator and Jerome: into thirst; the Chaldee: היך צחותא, like dryness; the Syriac: ܠܨܗܝܐ [III, 181] into dryness; the Arabic: عطش [ʿaṭash], thirst; the Ethiopic: ምጽማእ, a place of thirst. Again Isa 35:7: "And the parched place shall become a pool, וצמאון, and the thirsty place springs of water." Jerome: and the thirsty [ground]. Nor do the others render it much differently. The Greeks: τὴν διψῶσαν γῆν [tēn dipsōsan gēn]. The Arabic: الارض العطشانة [al-arḍ al-ʿaṭshāna], the thirsty land. The Chaldee: בית צחונא. The Syriac: ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ, a thirsty place. Moreover, in the very passage we are dealing with, absolutely all the translators understand the same thing, except Jerome alone. For none of them takes it here as the dipsas or any other kind of serpent. And what many write is false, that Jerome here follows the Greeks; for in them צמאון is not rendered διψὰς [dipsas], as these writers claim, but δίψα [dipsa], thirst; as in the Samaritan ࠑࠌࠀࠅࠍ and in both printed Arabic versions عطش [ʿaṭash], which likewise mean thirst; but in the MSS. مفازة [mafāza], and in both Chaldee versions בית צחונא, and in the Syriac ܒܝܬ ܨܗܘܢܐ, a thirsty place. Furthermore, after צמאון Moses adds by way of explanation [ἐπεξηγητικῶς, epexēgētikōs] אשר אין מים, that is, a thirsty place, in which there are no waters. So צמאון, with Moses himself as interpreter, is not the dipsas but a place in which there are no waters, which is the same as a thirsty place. The matter will be clearer from reading the whole period, which runs thus: "Who led you through the vast and terrible wilderness, in which were the prester and the scorpion; וצמאון, and through a thirsty place, in which there are no waters." That the period is to be divided thus is indicated by the accent Zakeph-Katon over the word עקרב, scorpion. But Jerome divides it after the word וצמאון, which he rendered and the dipsas. And he renders the following words אשר אין מים as and no waters at all, adding the little word and on his own, so that they would not be referred to the immediately preceding word; for these words would have made no sense: The dipsas, in which there are no waters. Finally, if צמאון were the dipsas, in the order of these words נחש שרף ועקרב וצמאון one might find fault with the fact that the scorpion is inserted between two species of serpents.
